body: What is the threshold for dark suns? Looking at your comparison images, `0.5` looks acceptable, for example. I think it would be best to minimize compatibility breakage (since there will be some regardless) and set the clamping value to the lowest value before the dark sun issue appears (which I suspect is just some epsilon greater than 0).

tbh, I am not sure if this change is even necessary. At the end of the day the sun color is a purely artistic choice. Could very well be that for some games having a dark sun might be part of the look the developer is going for. Unless this actually causes some crash or some serious artifacts I would argue to leave this the way it is.

Godot has plenty of other settings that can result in strange visuals when they are cranked to the extreme, and none of them have any built in hard limits unless things are actively breaking.

> Godot has plenty of other settings that can result in strange visuals when they are cranked to the extreme, and none of them have any built in hard limits unless things are actively breaking.

Yes, 100%.

And also, I believe that godotengine/godot-proposals#13748 clearly describes that this is not a scenario where the user is "cranking the settings to the extreme". The user simply wants to make the environment darker when the sun is setting, so they need to turn down their directional light energy and rely instead on ambient light and other light sources. This has the unfortunate and unintended consequence of making the sun turn dark/black.

The foundational issue here is that the sun colour is tied to the directional light energy in a non-physical way. This is a problematic design that doesn't work well with tonemapping, HDR, and generally lighting with a directional light. If we could go back in time, it would be better to have an entirely different design that gives artists control over the colour of their sun without needing to be scared of the colour changing to an unexpected colour just because they need to modulate the directional light energy of their scene. Or the automatic colour changes could be physically based instead.

> Looking at your comparison images, `0.5` looks acceptable, for example.

Art is a subjective thing, but this behaviour does not look good or reasonable to me: even when a sun changes colour as it sets, it never appears dark like this example.

For now, although this does change rendering behaviour, it addresses a unintentional consequence and problem of the original design in a way that is reasonable and doesn't break the visuals of games that are using it in the normal range where it behaves well.

I would wait and see if any users report issues with the current material before we go breaking compatibility to fix a hypothetical issue. 

ProceduralSkyMaterial is not intended to be realistic or have realistic behaviour. Behaving like a realistic sun + atmosphere is not a design goal. It is basically intended to allow you to place blobby colours in the sky as a placeholder.

I agree that tying the energy of the light source to its representation in the sky is not always wanted. But it hasn't been a significant problem in practice. Instead of breaking compatibility with the existing material, we should consider shipping an alternative if the demand is there. 

However, so far, only one person has expressed dissatisfaction with the current behaviour, so I really doubt the demand is there, either to justify breaking compatibility or to spend the time designing and shipping an alternative placeholder material.

Yeah, I agree with that. Given this behaviour has existed since 4.0 and only one person has reported the bug (and through a proposal instead of a bug report), it’s probably best left in its current state rather than trying to improve it.
